title: Giving Others What They Need to Save Face
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the sociological concept of 'face' -- self-image maintained in social settings -- and how it shapes people's reactions to criticism. It explains that people commonly protect face through excuses and justifications, and in extreme cases through anger or intimidation, when they feel their identity is threatened. The essay's core contribution is a technique: preceding feedback with a statement that affirms positive intentions or offers a reasonable account for the person's behavior, so the criticism lands without triggering a face-saving defensive reaction. Several sample phrasings illustrate the pattern in practice.
points: Face -- self-image in social settings -- is protected instinctively, often through excuses or justifications for one's behavior.
When a threat to self-identity feels extreme, people may defend face through anger, intimidation, or threats.
Good leaders presume self-image is always in play and are careful not to threaten it unnecessarily with criticism.
The best leaders 'give face' first -- affirming positive intent or offering a reasonable account -- before delivering criticism or direction.
Giving face allows a person to accept feedback while preserving their positive self-view, avoiding a defensive reaction.
quotes: Self-image, or face, is a powerful force in social settings.
Many of the most extreme episodes between people are a result of one party trying to save face.
Much of what we call emotional intelligence comes down to navigating the identity needs of others.
But the best leaders take this perceptive insight one step further. They give people face by reinforcing the positive view they have of themselves before they criticize them.
Doing so allows the person to maintain the positive image they have of themselves and accept the feedback without the need to save face.
The key to remember is that a person's self-image often determines how they respond.
